headline: Vibe Coding Has a Production Problem. A Cottage Industry Is Cashing In.
lede: AI-assisted development tools have made it startlingly easy to build a working prototype. Completing that prototype into a secure, scalable, app-store-approved product is a different discipline — one that has spawned an emerging category of consultancies promising to close the gap. Chris Maconi's Hechura is among the firms betting that the space between AI-generated demo and shippable software is wide enough to sustain a business.
body:
The tweet is, at its core, a sales pitch — but the problem it names is genuine. *Vibe coding*, the practice of describing software in plain language and letting an AI generate the implementation, has compressed the distance between idea and working prototype. The term was coined by Andrej Karpathy, the former Tesla and OpenAI researcher, who described the approach in early 2025 as “fully giving in to the vibes, embrace exponentials, forget that the code even exists.” Collins named it Word of the Year 2025. By 2026, roughly 92% of US developers report using AI coding tools daily, and an estimated 41% of all new code is AI-generated. The demo is cheap. The product is not.

The difficulty has a formal name in software engineering: the *Ninety-Ninety Rule*, attributed to Tom Cargill at Bell Labs: “the first 90 percent of the code accounts for the first 90 percent of the development time; the remaining 10 percent accounts for the other 90 percent.” Vibe coding has pushed an unusual cohort — entrepreneurs with product instincts but limited engineering depth — past the first threshold, leaving them stranded on the plateau. The missing 10% is precisely the hardest to prompt through: scalable data models, authorization logic, robust error handling, the *CI/CD* discipline that lets a team ship without breaking things.

Security is where the gap turns dangerous. Veracode's 2025 GenAI Code Security Report found that 45% of AI-generated code contains security flaws or bugs; the Cloud Security Alliance put the figure at 62% for design flaws or known vulnerabilities. The failure mode became concrete when a researcher disclosed CVE-2025-48757: 10.3% of applications built on Lovable, a popular vibe-coding platform, had critical misconfigurations in Supabase's *Row Level Security* — in some cases leaving API keys visible in browser developer tools. One vibe-coded social network, Moltbook, exposed 1.5 million authentication tokens and 35,000 email addresses within three days of launch. Django co-creator Simon Willison warned publicly that the industry is “due a Challenger disaster with respect to coding agent security.”

Apple (AAPL) has responded to the flood of AI-built submissions with tightening enforcement. App Store submissions surged roughly 84% in a single quarter after vibe coding went mainstream; Apple was reviewing some 200,000 submissions weekly at peak 2025 volume. The company tightened enforcement of Guideline 2.5.2, which prohibits apps that download or execute code after review, and blocked updates for several AI coding environments — including Replit — in early 2026. The most common rejection reasons for AI-built apps (minimum functionality, web-wrapper detection, missing privacy policies) map almost perfectly onto the gaps that experienced engineers catch before submission.

Into this gap steps a small but proliferating category of service providers. **Hechura**, run by Maconi — a 26-year veteran with three prior CTO exits — offers a two-week, $10,000 fixed-price sprint, “CTO-led, AI-native,” with clients retaining full code ownership. Add Jam, a Glasgow-based equivalent, pitches essentially the same positioning. The pitch practically writes itself. The risk for buyers is that the sellers are self-selected participants in the same AI wave whose own engineering rigor is unverified. Hechura's listing on Clutch, a B2B software-review platform, carries two reviews averaging 3.5 out of 5; one cites “security vulnerabilities in the final product” — a notable caveat for a firm that explicitly markets hardening as a core service.

concepts.definition: A software development approach in which the programmer describes desired functionality in plain language and lets an AI model generate the implementation code. Coined by Andrej Karpathy in early 2025, it lowers the barrier to building working prototypes but typically produces code that requires significant hardening before production deployment.

An aphorism from Bell Labs researcher Tom Cargill, published in 1985: the first 90% of the code takes 90% of the development time; the remaining 10% takes another 90%. It captures the consistent underestimation of the work needed to complete, test, and harden software — particularly the non-functional requirements that emerge only under real usage.

A database access-control feature that restricts which rows a given user or role can read, write, or delete — enforced at the database engine rather than in application code. When disabled or misconfigured (as in the Lovable/Supabase incident), it can expose entire tables of user data to anyone with database credentials.

Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery: automated pipelines that build, test, and deploy code on every change. CI catches integration errors early; CD automates the release process. Absent CI/CD, teams typically rely on manual testing and infrequent, higher-risk deployments — a common gap in vibe-coded projects.

fact_check: The tweet's accompanying image was OCR-read as “iXtech,” but no company by that name connected to Chris Maconi can be independently verified. Maconi's operating entity is Hechura (hechura.co), a boutique founded in April 2024. The OCR may have misread the branding, or iXtech could be an unindexed trade name. Separately, the tweet's implicit claim that Hechura reliably delivers production-grade, secure code is complicated by a third-party Clutch review citing “security vulnerabilities in the final product” — the same category of failure the service markets itself as preventing.
